doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jackie McLean, Sonny Rollins and avoiding junkies
summary: He lived near McLean and Rollins but kept his distance from addicts.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Back to alto players, did you get to know Jackie McLean well?
I knew Jackie McLean well. He was like a brother.
When did you meet him? When you got to New York?

Yeah. I lived up there. I lived on 155th. He lived on 158th. Sonny Rollins lived around the corner. Edgecombe Avenue. I’d see all of them. But these guys were junkies. They were junkies. Sorry to say, but I had no use for no junkies. Because I thought it would just be my luck to be talking to one of them and the police run up and get us—get everybody.
You thought you’d be caught in the same net, you mean?
You got it. Because all they did was hustle every day to try to get money, to get high. They had some musical talent. But they’re characters that I wouldn’t recommend.
Now, people did change and get over their habits.
I don’t know. I doubt it.
When did you first meet someone who was strung out on drugs?
When did I first MEET someone?

Oh, no. No drugs in North Carolina. They’d give you thirty years for smoking weed down there. They didn’t have no junkies in North Carolina, not when I was there. When I got to New York, I saw plenty of junkies.
So your attitude towards people who were abusing drugs was more based on self- preservation, it sounds like, than anything else...
